title: Valence number
competency: Define valence as the combining power of an atom.

keywords.def: The combining power of an element. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.
An atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.

en.text: The combining power of an element is its valence. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3. Iron, copper, lead and tin have more than one valence. The charge on an ion equals its valence: Cl⁻ has 1, O²⁻ has 2, Al³⁺ has 3.

screens.title: Joining power
screens.ask: Hydrogen joins one other atom. Oxygen can join two hydrogens in H₂O. Which has more "joining power"?
screens.after: Oxygen holds two hydrogens, so it has more combining power. This power is called valence.

screens.title: 3.2.3 Valence number
paras: Each element in a compound has a combining power.
The combining power of an element is called valence.
If we know the valences, it is easy to write a formula.
Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.

screens.title: More than one valence
paras: Some elements have more than one valence.
Iron, copper, lead and tin are common examples.
Ions are atoms with a positive or negative charge.
The charge an ion carries equals its valence. Cl⁻, O²⁻ and Al³⁺ have valences 1, 2 and 3.

screens.text: What is the valence of oxygen?
screens.why: Table 3.4 puts oxygen in the valence 2 column.
screens.clue: Look at the non-metal row of Table 3.4.

screens.text: What is the valence of aluminium?
screens.why: Al is in the valence 3 column; Al³⁺ carries 3 charges.
screens.clue: Look at the charge on Al³⁺.

screens.text: Iron has only one valence number.
screens.why: Iron has valence 2, iron(II), and valence 3, iron(III).

screens.text: An ion has the charge 2−. What is its valence?
screens.why: The valence equals the number of charges, not the sign. 2− means valence 2, like O²⁻.
